entries.8514bfe6998413357d8df878bd3593899172efec: <div sID="gen6283" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="2Sam.16" sID="2Sam.16"/> <div eID="gen6283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6284" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6285" type="x-p"/> In the close of the foregoing chapter we left David flying from Jerusalem, and Absalom entering into it; in this chapter, I. We are to follow David in his melancholy flight; and there we find him, 1. Cheated by Ziba, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.1-2Sam.16.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. 2. Cursed by Shimei, which he bears with wonderful patience, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5-2Sam.16.14">ver. 5-14</reference>. II. We are to meet Absalom in his triumphant entry; and there we find him, 1. Cheated by Hushai, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.15-2Sam.16.19">ver. 15-19</reference>. 2. Counselled by Ahithophel to go in unto his father's concubines, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.20-2Sam.16.23">ver. 20-23</reference>.
entries.531f316c213e96c7fa451f2a6f9682a691e7e7e7: <div eID="gen6285" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6284" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ziba's Calumny. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6286" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And when David was a little past the top <hi type="italic">of the hill,</hi> behold, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him, with a couple of asses saddled, and upon them two hundred <hi type="italic">loaves</hi> of bread, and a hundred bunches of raisins, and a hundred of summer fruits, and a bottle of wine. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the king said unto Ziba, What meanest thou by these? And Ziba said, The asses <hi type="italic">be</hi> for the king's household to ride on; and the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat; and the wine, that such as be faint in the wilderness may drink. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the king said, And where <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy master's son? And Ziba said unto the king, Behold, he abideth at Jerusalem: for he said, To day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then said the king to Ziba, Behold, thine <hi type="italic">are</hi> all that <hi type="italic">pertained</hi> unto Mephibosheth. And Ziba said, I humbly beseech thee <hi type="italic">that</hi> I may find grace in thy sight, my lord, O king. <div eID="gen6286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6287" type="x-p"/> We read before how kind David was to Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, how he prudently entrusted his servant Ziba with the management of his estate, while he generously entertained him at his own table, <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.10">ch. ix. 10</reference>. This matter was well settled; but, it seems, Ziba is not content to be manager, he longs to be master, of Mephibosheth's estate. Now, he thinks, is his time to make himself so; if he can procure a grant of it from the crown, whether David or Absalom get the better it is all one to him, he hopes he shall secure his prey, which he promises himself by fishing in troubled waters. In order hereunto, 1. He made David a handsome present of provisions, which was the more welcome because it came seasonably (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.1">v. 1</reference>), and with this he designed to incline him to himself; for <hi type="italic">a man's gift maketh room for him, and bringeth him before great men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.16">Prov. xviii. 16</reference>. Nay, <hi type="italic">Whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.8">Prov. xvii. 8</reference>. David inferred from this that Ziba was a very discreet and generous man, and well affected to him, when, in all, he designed nothing but to make his own market and to get Mephibosheth's estate settled upon himself. Shall the prospect of advantage in this world make men generous to the rich? and shall not the belief of an abundant recompence in the resurrection of the just make us charitable to the poor? <reference osisRef="Luke.14.14">Luke xiv. 14</reference>. Ziba was very considerate in the present he brought to David; it was what would do him some good in his present distress, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.2">v. 2</reference>. Observe, The wine was intended for those that were faint, not for the king's own drinking, or the courtiers; it seems, they did not commonly use it, but it was for cordials for those <hi type="italic">that were ready to perish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.6">Prov. xxxi. 6</reference>. Blessed art thou, O land! when thy princes use wine for strength, as David did, and not for drunkenness, as Absalom did, <reference osisRef="2Sam.18.28">ch. xiii. 28</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.17">Eccl. x. 17</reference>. Whatever Ziba intended in this present, God's providence sent it to David for his support very graciously. God makes use of bad men for good purposes to his people, and sends them meat by ravens. Having by his present insinuated himself into David's affection, and gained credit with him, the next thing he has to do for the compassing of his end is to incense him against Mephibosheth, which he does by a false accusation, representing him as ungratefully designing to raise himself by the present broils, and to recover the crown to his own head, now that David and his son were contending for it. David enquires for him as one of his family, which gives Ziba occasion to tell this false story of him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.3">v. 3</reference>. What immense damages do masters often sustain by the lying tongues of their servants! David knew Mephibosheth not to be an ambitious man, but easy in his place, and well-affected to him and his government; nor could he be so weak as to expect with his lame legs to climb the ladder of preferment; yet David gives credit to the calumny, and, without further enquiry or consideration, convicts Mephibosheth of treason, seizes his lands as forfeited, and grants them to Ziba: <hi type="italic">Behold, thine are all that pertained to Mephibosheth</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.4">v. 4</reference>), a rash judgment, and which afterwards he was ashamed of, when the truth came to light, <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.29">ch. xix. 29</reference>. Princes cannot help it, but they will be sometimes (as our law speaks) deceived in their grants; but they ought to use all means possible to discover the truth and to guard against malicious designing men, who would impose upon them, as Ziba did upon David. Having by his wiles gained his point, Ziba secretly laughed at the king's credulity, congratulated himself on his success, and departed, with a great compliment upon the king, that he valued his favour more than Mephibosheth's estate: "Let me <hi type="italic">find grace in thy sight, O king!</hi> and I have enough." Great men ought always to be jealous of flatterers, and remember that nature has given them two ears, that they may hear both sides.
entries.b3e6a7ed42cdab11e44f622bbdd705e0a8635842: <div eID="gen6287" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Cursed by Shimei. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6288" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And when king David came to Bahurim, behold, thence came out a man of the family of the house of Saul, whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Shimei, the son of Gera: he came forth, and cursed still as he came. <hi type="super">6</hi> And he cast stones at David, and at all the servants of king David: and all the people and all the mighty men <hi type="italic">were</hi> on his right hand and on his left. <hi type="super">7</hi> And thus said Shimei when he cursed, Come out, come out, thou bloody man, and thou man of Belial: <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath returned upon thee all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose stead thou hast reigned; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom thy son: and, behold, thou <hi type="italic">art taken</hi> in thy mischief, because thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> a bloody man. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then said Abishai the son of Zeruiah unto the king, Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? let me go over, I pray thee, and take off his head. <hi type="super">10</hi> And the king said, What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah? so let him curse, because the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath said unto him, Curse David. Who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so? <hi type="super">11</hi> And David said to Abishai, and to all his servants, Behold, my son, which came forth of my bowels, seeketh my life: how much more now <hi type="italic">may this</hi> Benjamite <hi type="italic">do it?</hi> let him alone, and let him curse; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath bidden him. <hi type="super">12</hi> It may be that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will look on mine affliction, and that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will requite me good for his cursing this day. <hi type="super">13</hi> And as David and his men went by the way, Shimei went along on the hill's side over against him, and cursed as he went, and threw stones at him, and cast dust. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the king, and all the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, came weary, and refreshed themselves there. <div eID="gen6288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6289" type="x-p"/> We here find how David bore Shimei's curses much better than he had borne Ziba's flatteries. By the latter he was brought to pass a wrong judgment on another, by the former to pass a right judgment on himself. The world's smiles are more dangerous than its frowns. Observe here, <div eID="gen6289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6290" type="x-p"/> I. How insolent and furious Shimei was, and how his malice took occasion from David's present distress to be so much the more outrageous. David, in his flight, had come to Bahurim, a city of Benjamin in or near which this Shimei lived, who, being of the house of Saul (with the fall of which all his hopes of preferment fell), had an implacable enmity to David, unjustly looking upon him as the ruin of Saul and his family only because, by the divine appointment, he succeeded Saul. While David was in prosperity and power, Shimei hated him as much as he did now, but he durst not then say anything against him. God knows what is in the hearts of those that are disaffected to him and his government, but earthly princes do not. Now he came forth, and cursed David with all the bad words and wishes he could invent, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5">v. 5</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen6290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6291" type="x-p"/> 1. Why he took this opportunity to give vent to his malice. (1.) Because now he thought he might do it safely; yet, if David had thought proper to resent the provocation, it would have cost Shimei his life. (2.) Because now it would be most grievous to David, would add affliction to his grief, and pour vinegar into his wounds. He complains of those as most barbarous who <hi type="italic">talk to the grief of those whom God has wounded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.26">Ps. lxix. 26</reference>. So Shimei did, loading him with curses whom no generous eye could look upon without compassion. (3.) Because now he thought that Providence justified his reproaches, and that David's present afflictions proved him to be as bad a man as he was willing to represent him. Job's friends condemned him upon this false principle. Those that are under the rebukes of a gracious God must not think it strange if these bring upon them the reproaches of evil men. If once it be said, <hi type="italic">God hath forsaken him,</hi> presently it follows, <hi type="italic">Persecute and take him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.71.11">Ps. lxxi. 11</reference>. But it is the character of a base spirit thus to trample upon those that are down, and insult over them. <div eID="gen6291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6292" type="x-p"/> 2. How his malice was expressed. See, (1.) What this wretched man did: <hi type="italic">He cast stones at David</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.6">v. 6</reference>), as if his king had been a dog, or the worst of criminals, whom all Israel must stone with stones till he die. Perhaps he kept at such a distance that the stones he threw could not reach David, nor any of his attendants, yet he showed what he would have done if it had been in his power. <hi type="italic">He cast dust</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.13">v. 13</reference>), which, probably, would blow into his own eyes, like the curses he threw, which, being causeless, would return upon his own head. Thus, while his malice made him odious, the impotency of it made him ridiculous and contemptible. Those that fight against God cannot hurt him, though they hate him. <hi type="italic">If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.35.6">Job xxxv. 6</reference>. It was an aggravation of his wickedness that David was attended with his mighty men on his right hand and on his left, so that he was not in so forlorn a condition as he thought (<hi type="italic">persecuted but not forsaken</hi>), and that he continued to do it, and did it the more passionately, for David's bearing it patiently. (2.) What he said. With the stones he shot his arrows, even bitter words (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.7-2Sam.16.8">v. 7, 8</reference>), in contempt of that law, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not curse the gods,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.22.28">Exod. xxii. 28</reference>. David was a man of honour and conscience, and in great reputation for every thing that was just and good; what could this foul mouth say against him? Why, truly, what was done long since to the house of Saul was the only thing which he could recollect, and with this he upbraided David because it was the thing that he himself was a loser by. See how apt we are to judge of men and their character by what they are to us, and to conclude that those are certainly evil men that have ever so justly been, or that we ever so unjustly think have been, instruments of evil to us. So partial are we to ourselves that no rule can be more fallacious than this. No man could be more innocent of the blood of the house of Saul than David was. Once and again he spared Saul's life, while Saul sought his. When Saul and his sons were slain by the Philistines, David and his men were many miles off; and, when they heard it, they lamented it. From the murder of Abner and Ish-bosheth he had sufficiently cleared himself; and yet all <hi type="italic">the blood of the house of Saul</hi> must be laid at his door. Innocency is no fence against malice and falsehood; nor are we to think it strange if we be charged with that from which we have been most careful to keep ourselves. It is well for us that men are not to be our judges, but he whose judgment is according to truth. The blood of the house of Saul is here most unjustly charged upon David, [1.] As that which gave him his character, and denominated him a bloody man and a man of Belial, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.7">v. 7</reference>. And, if a man of blood, no doubt a man of Belial, that is, a child of the devil, who is called <hi type="italic">Belial</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.15">2 Cor. vi. 15</reference>), and who was a murderer from the beginning. Bloody men are the worst of men. [2.] As that which brought the present trouble upon him: "Now that thou art dethroned, and driven out to the wilderness, <hi type="italic">the Lord has returned upon thee the blood of the house of Saul.</hi>" See how forward malicious men are to press God's judgments into the service of their own passion and revenge. If any who have, as they think, wronged them, should come into trouble, the injury done to them must be made the cause of the trouble. But we must take heed lest we wrong God by making his providence thus to patronise our foolish and unjust resentments. As the <hi type="italic">wrath of man works not the righteousness of God,</hi> so the righteousness of God serves not the wrath of man. [3.] As that which would now be his utter ruin; for he endeavours to make him despair of ever recovering his throne again. Now they said, <hi type="italic">There is no help for him in God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.3.2">Ps. iii. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">the Lord hath delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom</hi> (not Mephibosheth—the house of Saul never dreamed of making <hi type="italic">him</hi> king, as Ziba suggested), <hi type="italic">and thou art taken in thy mischief,</hi> that is, "the mischief that will be thy destruction, and all because thou art a bloody man." Thus Shimei cursed. <div eID="gen6292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6293" type="x-p"/> II. See how patient and submissive David was under this abuse. The sons of Zeruiah, Abishai particularly, were forward to maintain David's honour with their swords; they resented the affront keenly, as well they might: <hi type="italic">Why should this dead dog</hi> be suffered to <hi type="italic">curse the king?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.9">v. 9</reference>. If David will but give them leave, they will put these lying cursing lips to silence, and take off his head; for his throwing stones at the king was an overt act, which abundantly proved that he compassed and imagined his death. But the king would by no means suffer it: <hi type="italic">What have I to do with you? So let him curse.</hi> Thus Christ rebuked the disciples, who, in zeal for his honour, would have commanded fire from heaven on the town that affronted him, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.55">Luke ix. 55</reference>. Let us see with what considerations David quieted himself. 1. The chief thing that silenced him was that he had deserved this affliction. This is not mentioned indeed; for a man may truly repent, and yet needs not, upon all occasions, proclaim his penitent reflections. Shimei unjustly upbraided him with the blood of Saul: from <hi type="italic">that</hi> his conscience acquitted him, but, at the same time, it charged him with the blood of Uriah. "The reproach is too true" (thinks David), "though false as he means it." Note, A humble tender spirit will turn reproaches into reproofs, and so get good by them, instead of being provoked by them. 2. He observes the hand of God in it: <hi type="italic">The Lord hath said unto him, Curse David</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.10">v. 10</reference>), and again, <hi type="italic">So let him curse, for the Lord hath bidden him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.11">v. 11</reference>. As it was Shimei's sin, it was not from God, but from the devil and his own wicked heart, nor did God's hand in it excuse or extenuate it, much less justify it, any more than it did the sin of those who put Christ to death, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.4.28">iv. 28</reference>. But, as it was David's affliction, it was from the Lord, one of the evils which he raised up against him. David looked above the instrument of his trouble to the supreme director, as Job, when the plunderers had stripped him, acknowledged, <hi type="italic">The Lord hath taken away.</hi> Nothing more proper to quiet a gracious soul under affliction than an eye to the hand of God in it. <hi type="italic">I opened not my mouth, because thou didst it.</hi> The scourge of the tongue is God's rod. 3. He quiets himself under the less affliction with the consideration of the greater (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">My son seeks my life, much more may this Benjamite.</hi> Note, Tribulation works patience in those that are sanctified. The more we bear the better able we should be to bear still more; what tries our patience should improve it. The more we are inured to trouble the less we should be surprised at it, and not think it strange. Marvel not that enemies are injurious, when even friends are unkind; nor that friends are unkind, when even children are undutiful. 4. He comforts himself with hopes that God would, in some way or other, bring good to him out of his affliction, would balance the trouble itself, and recompense his patience under it: "<hi type="italic">The Lord will requite me good for his cursing.</hi> If God bid Shimei grieve me, it is that he himself may the more sensibly comfort me; surely he has mercy in store for me, which he is preparing me for by this trial." We may depend upon God as our pay-master, not only for our services, but for our sufferings. <hi type="italic">Let them curse, but bless thou.</hi> David, at length, is housed at Bahurim (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.14">v. 14</reference>), where he meets with refreshment, and is hidden from this strife of tongues.
entries.e576e21d4adcb66d00c64e30f4cb17def43f118b: <div eID="gen6293" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Hushai Deceives Absalom; Ahithophel's Wicked Counsel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1023.)</title> <div sID="gen6294" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And Absalom, and all the people the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him. <hi type="super">16</hi> And it came to pass, when Hushai the Archite, David's friend, was come unto Absalom, that Hushai said unto Absalom, God save the king, God save the king. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Absalom said to Hushai, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> this thy kindness to thy friend? why wentest thou not with thy friend? <hi type="super">18</hi> And Hushai said unto Absalom, Nay; but whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and this people, and all the men of Israel, choose, his will I be, and with him will I abide. <hi type="super">19</hi> And again, whom should I serve? <hi type="italic">should I</hi> not <hi type="italic">serve</hi> in the presence of his son? as I have served in thy father's presence, so will I be in thy presence. <hi type="super">20</hi> Then said Absalom to Ahithophel, Give counsel among you what we shall do. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Ahithophel said unto Absalom, Go in unto thy father's concubines, which he hath left to keep the house; and all Israel shall hear that thou art abhorred of thy father: then shall the hands of all that <hi type="italic">are</hi> with thee be strong. <hi type="super">22</hi> So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel. <hi type="super">23</hi> And the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, <hi type="italic">was</hi> as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God: so <hi type="italic">was</hi> all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom. <div eID="gen6294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6295" type="x-p"/> Absalom had notice sent him speedily by some of his friends at Jerusalem that David had withdrawn, and with what a small retinue he had gone; so that the coasts were clear, Absalom might take possession of Jerusalem when he pleased. The gates were open, and there was none to oppose him. Accordingly he came without delay (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.15">v. 15</reference>), extremely elevated, no doubt, with this success at first, and that that in which, when he formed his design, he probably apprehended the greatest difficulty, was so easily and effectually done. Now that he is master of Jerusalem he concludes all his own, the country will follow of course. God suffers wicked men to prosper awhile in their wicked plots, even beyond their expectation, that their disappointment may be the more grievous and disgraceful. The most celebrated politicians of that age were Ahithophel and Hushai. The former Absalom brings with him to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.15">v. 15</reference>), the other meets him there (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.16">v. 16</reference>), so that he cannot but think himself sure of success, when he has both these to be his counsellors; on them he relies, and consults not the ark, though he has that with him. But miserable counsellors were they both; for, <div eID="gen6295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6296" type="x-p"/> I. Hushai would never counsel him to do wisely. He was really his enemy, and designed to betray him, while he pretended to be in his interest; so that Absalom could not have a more dangerous man about him. 1. Hushai complimented him upon his accession to the throne, as if he had been abundantly satisfied in this title, and well pleased that he had come to the possession, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.16">v. 16</reference>. What arts of dissimulation are those tempted to use who govern themselves by fleshly wisdom! and how happy are those who have not known these depths of Satan, but have their conversation in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity! 2. Absalom was surprised to find <hi type="italic">him</hi> for him who was known to be David's intimate friend and confidant. He asks him, <hi type="italic">Is this thy kindness to thy friend?</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.17">v. 17</reference>), pleasing himself with this thought, that all would be his, since Hushai was. He doubts not of his sincerity, but easily believes what he wishes to be true, that David's best friends are so in love with himself as to take the first opportunity to declare for him, <hi type="italic">though the pride of his heart deceived him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Obad.1.3">Obad. 3</reference>. Hushai confirmed him in the belief that he was hearty for him. For, though David is his friend, yet he is for the king in <hi type="italic">possession,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.18">v. 18</reference>. Whom the people choose, and Providence smiles upon, he will be faithful to; and he is for the king in <hi type="italic">succession</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.19">v. 19</reference>), the rising sun. It was true, he loved his father; but he had had his day, and it was over; and why should he not love his successor as well? Thus he pretended to give reasons for a resolution he abhorred the thought of. <div eID="gen6296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6297" type="x-p"/> II. Ahithophel counselled him to do wickedly, and so did as effectually betray him as he did who was designedly false to him; for those that advise men to sin certainly advise them to their hurt; and that government which is founded in sin is founded in the sand. <div eID="gen6297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6298" type="x-p"/> 1. It seems, Ahithophel was noted as a deep politician; his counsel was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.23">v. 23</reference>. Such reputation was he in for subtlety and sagacity in public affairs, such reaches had he beyond other privy-counselors, such reasons would he give for his advice, and such success generally his projects had, that all people, good and bad, both David and Absalom, had a profound regard for his sentiments, too much by far, when they regarded him <hi type="italic">as an oracle of God;</hi> shall the prudence of any mortal compare with him who only is wise? Let us observe from this account of Ahithophel's fame for policy, (1.) That many excel in worldly wisdom who are utterly destitute of heavenly grace, because those who set up for oracles themselves are apt to despise the oracles of God. <hi type="italic">God has chosen the foolish things of the world;</hi> and the greatest statesmen are seldom the greatest saints. (2.) That frequently the greatest politicians act most foolishly for themselves. Ahithophel was cried up for an oracle, and yet very unwisely took part with Absalom, who was not only a usurper, but a rash youth, never likely to come to good, whose fall, and the fall of all that adhered to him, any one, with the tenth part of the policy that Ahithophel pretended to, might foresee. Well, after all, honesty is the best policy, and will be found so in the long run. But, <div eID="gen6298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6299" type="x-p"/> 2. His policy in this case defeated its own aim. Observe, <div eID="gen6299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6300" type="x-p"/> (1.) The wicked counsel Ahithophel gave to Absalom. Finding that David had left his concubines to keep the house, he advised him to <hi type="italic">lie with them</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.16.21">v. 21</reference>), a very wicked thing. The divine law had made it a capital crime, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.11">Lev. xx. 11</reference>. The apostle speaks of it as a piece of villany <hi type="italic">not so much as named among the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.1">1 Cor. v. 1</reference>. Reuben lost his birthright for it. But Ahithophel advised Absalom to it as a public thing, because it would give assurance to all Israel, [1.] That he was in good earnest in his pretensions. No doubt he resolved to make himself master of all that belonged to his predecessor when he began with his concubines. [2.] That he was resolved never to make peace with his father upon any terms; for by this he would render himself so odious to his father that he would never be reconciled to him, which perhaps the people were jealous of and that they must be sacrificed to the reconciliation. Having drawn the sword, he did, by this provocation, throw away the scabbard, which would strengthen the hands of his party and keep them firmly to him. This was Ahithophel's cursed policy, which bespoke him rather <hi type="italic">an oracle of devil than of God.</hi> <div eID="gen6300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6301" type="x-p"/> (2.) Absalom's compliance with this counsel. It entirely suited his lewd and wicked mind, and he delayed not to put it in execution, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.22">v. 22</reference>. When an unnatural rebellion was the opera, what fitter prologue could there be to it than such unnatural lust? Thus was his wickedness all of a piece, and such as a conscience not quite seared could not entertain the thoughts of without the utmost horror. Nay, the client outdoes what his counsel advises. Ahithophel advised him to do it, that all Israel shall <hi type="italic">see</hi> it. A tent is accordingly spread on the top of the house for the purpose; so impudently does he declare his sin as Sodom. Yet, in this, the word of God was fulfilled in the letter of it: God had threatened, by Nathan, that, for defiling Bath-sheba, David should have his own wives publicly debauched (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.11-2Sam.12.12">ch. xii. 11, 12</reference>), and some think that Ahithophel, in advising it, designed to be revenged on David for the injury done to Bath-sheba, who was his grand-daughter: for she was the daughter of Eliam (<reference osisRef="2Sam.11.3">ch. xi. 3</reference>), who was the son of Ahithophel, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.34">ch. xxiii. 34</reference>. Job speaks of this as the just punishment of adultery (<hi type="italic">Let my wife grind to another,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.9-Job.31.10">Job xxxi. 9, 10</reference>), and the prophet, <reference osisRef="Hos.4.13-Hos.4.14">Hos. iv. 13, 14</reference>. What to think of these concubines, who submitted to this wickedness, I know not; but how unrighteous soever Absalom and they were, we must say, <hi type="italic">The Lord is righteous:</hi> nor shall any word of his fall to the ground.  <chapter eID="2Sam.16"/> <div eID="gen6301" type="x-p"/>

entries.22ef56cc3e1074924fd54cff8919541c85e56abb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2967"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <div sID="gen4099" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.1-2Sam.16.4">2Sa 16:1-4</reference>. Ziba, by False Suggestions, Claims His Master's Inheritance.<div eID="gen4099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4100" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2967"/><hi type="bold">1. Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him--</hi>This crafty man, anticipating the certain failure of Absalom's conspiracy, took steps to prepare for his future advancement on the restoration of the king.<div eID="gen4100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a bottle of wine--</hi>a large goatskin vessel. Its size made the supply of wine proportioned to the rest of his present. <div eID="gen4101" type="x-p"/>
entries.c92f9351a6839bb8bd9af9717be074a30f0d0569: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2968"/><div sID="gen4102" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2968"/><hi type="bold">2. The asses be for the king's household to ride on--</hi>The royal fugitives were moving on foot, not from inability to procure conveyances, but as being suitable to their present state of humiliation and penitence. <div eID="gen4102" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c976bd7a785fabd21466c7eea133b305387337f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2969"/><div sID="gen4103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2969"/><hi type="bold">3. To-day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father--</hi>Such a hope might not unnaturally arise at this period of civil distraction, that the family of David would destroy themselves by their mutual broils, and the people reinstate the old dynasty. There was an air of plausibility in Ziba's story. Many, on whom the king had conferred favors, were now deserting him. No wonder, therefore, that in the excitement of momentary feeling, believing, on the report of a slanderer, Mephibosheth to be among the number, he pronounced a rash and unrighteous judgment by which a great injury was inflicted on the character and interests of a devoted friend.<div eID="gen4103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4104" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5-2Sam.16.19">2Sa 16:5-19</reference>. Shimei Curses David. <div eID="gen4104" type="x-p"/>
entries.2cbb18ffd45dfd342d00afe2d355f20016b00e2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2970"/><div sID="gen4105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2970"/><hi type="bold">5-12. when king David came to Bahurim--</hi>a city of Benjamin (<reference osisRef="2Sam.3.16">2Sa 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.16">19:16</reference>). It is, however, only the confines of the district that are here meant.<div eID="gen4105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shimei, ... a man of the family of Saul--</hi>The misfortune of his family, and the occupation by David of what they considered their rightful possessions, afforded a natural, if not a justifiable cause for this ebullition of rude insults and violence. He upbraided David as an ambitious usurper, and charged him, as one whose misdeeds had recoiled upon his own head, to surrender a throne to which he was not entitled. His language was that of a man incensed by the wrongs that he conceived had been done to his house. David was guiltless of the crime of which Shimei accused him; but his conscience reminded him of other flagrant iniquities; and he, therefore, regarded the cursing of this man as a chastisement from heaven. His answer to Abishai's proposal evinced the spirit of deep and humble resignation--the spirit of a man who watched the course of Providence, and acknowledged Shimei as the instrument of God's chastening hand. One thing is remarkable, that he acted more independently of the sons of Zeruiah in this season of great distress than he could often muster courage to do in the days of his prosperity and power. <div eID="gen4106" type="x-p"/>
entries.652e0a78dd5e4c478e96ac7b76985a6ed517e2dd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2971"/><div sID="gen4107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2971"/><hi type="bold">13. went along on the hill's side over against him--</hi>as he descended the rough road on the eastern side of the Mount of Olives, "went along on the hill's side"--literally, "the rib of the hill."<div eID="gen4107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">threw stones at him--</hi>as a mark of contempt and insult.<div eID="gen4108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast dust--</hi>As if to add insult to injury, clouds of dust were thrown by this disloyal subject in the path of his unfortunate sovereign. <div eID="gen4109" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c277f34b1d1e5b70cd53445239b5cb49a33bae9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2972"/><div sID="gen4110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2972"/><hi type="bold">14. refreshed themselves there--</hi>that is, in the city of Bahurim. <div eID="gen4110" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7ff45c0d292cd5a97684b09edcd4295855e2e75: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2973"/><div sID="gen4111" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2973"/><hi type="bold">15-19. Hushai said unto Absalom, God save the king--</hi>Hushai's devotion to David was so well-known, that his presence in the camp of the conspirators excited great surprise. Professing, however, with great address, to consider it his duty to support the cause which the course of Providence and the national will had seemingly decreed should triumph, and urging his friendship for the father as a ground of confidence in his fidelity to the son, he persuaded Absalom of his sincerity, and was admitted among the councillors of the new king.<div eID="gen4111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4112" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.20-2Sam.16.23">2Sa 16:20-23</reference>. Ahithophel's Counsel. <div eID="gen4112" type="x-p"/>
entries.c014a8369b84b2202764909c610388a0d4eb7ab9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2974"/><div sID="gen4113" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2974"/><hi type="bold">20. Give counsel among you what we shall do--</hi>This is the first cabinet council on record, although the deference paid to Ahithophel gave him the entire direction of the proceedings. <div eID="gen4113" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2d3c0456bd29929a259c363c39e2609d69c273f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2975"/><div sID="gen4114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2975"/><hi type="bold">21. Ahithophel said unto Absalom--</hi>This councillor saw that now the die was cast; half measures would be inexpedient. To cut off all possibility of reconciliation between the king and his rebellious son, he gave this atrocious advice regarding the treatment of the royal women who had been left in charge of the palace. Women, being held sacred, are generally left inviolate in the casualties of war. The history of the East affords only one parallel to this infamous outrage of Absalom. <chapter eID="2Sam.16"/>

entries.79ff99686c2fcd2ebac32bf7ec50867f539a5a37: <div eID="gen11122" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen11123" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11124" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11124" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11123" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11125" type="x-p"/> Ziba, servant of Mephibosheth, meets David with provisions, and by false insinuations obtains the grant of his masters property, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.1-2Sam.16.4">2Sam 16:1-4</reference>. Shimei abuses and curses David, who restrains Abishai from slaying him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5-2Sam.16.14">2Sam 16:5-14</reference>. Hushai makes a feigned tender of his services to Absalom, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.15-2Sam.16.19">2Sam 16:15-19</reference>. Absalom calls a council and Ahithophel advises him to go in to his father's concubines, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.20-2Sam.16.22">2Sam 16:20-22</reference>. Character of Ahithophel as a counselor, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.23">2Sam 16:23</reference>. <div eID="gen11125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11126" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen11126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11127" type="x-p"/> Two hundred loaves of bread - The word loaf gives us a false idea of the ancient Jewish bread; it was thin cakes, not yeasted and raised like ours. <div eID="gen11127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11128" type="x-p"/> Bunches of raisins - See on <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.18">1Sam 25:18</reference> (note). <div eID="gen11128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11129" type="x-p"/> Summer fruits - These were probably pumpions, cucumbers, or watermelons. The two latter are extensively used in those countries to refresh travelers in the burning heat of the summer. Mr. Harmer supposes they are called summer fruits on this very account. <div eID="gen11129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11130" type="x-p"/> A bottle of wine - A goat's skin full of wine; this I have already shown was the general bottle in the Eastern countries; see on <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.18">1Sam 25:18</reference> (note).
entries.9d3f8dae86aed989ba655922845a11e6d3ea89b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen11130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11131" type="x-p"/> The asses be for the king's household - This is the Eastern method of speaking when any thing is presented to a great man: "This and this is for the slaves of the servants of your majesty," when at the same time the presents are intended for the sovereign himself, and are so understood. It is a high Eastern compliment: These presents are not worthy of your acceptance; they are only fit for the slaves of your slaves.
entries.aaf8e14bce0bde7f21cb14792d5ed3d4a226674f: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen11131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11132" type="x-p"/> To-day shall the house of Israel - What a base wretch was Ziba! and how unfounded was this accusation against the peaceable, loyal and innocent Mephibosheth!
entries.c272c3cfb4b8223f340d1b1b2b7fbd14ff51edd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen11132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11133" type="x-p"/> Thine are all - This conduct of David was very rash; he spoiled an honorable man to reward a villain, not giving himself time to look into the circumstances of the case. But David was in heavy afflictions, and these sometimes make even a wise man mad. Nothing should be done rashly; he who is in the habit of obeying the first impulse of his passions or feelings, will seldom do a right action, and never keep a clear conscience.
entries.f3a18b5866dde86d352e037f9d52e6ad8d76d30c: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen11133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11134" type="x-p"/> David came to Bahurim - This place lay northward of Jerusalem, in the tribe of Benjamin. It is called Almon, <reference osisRef="Jos.21.18">Jos 21:18</reference>; and Alemeth, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.60">1Chr 6:60</reference>. Bahurim signifies youths, and Almuth youth; so the names are of the same import. <div eID="gen11134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11135" type="x-p"/> Cursed still as he came - Used imprecations and execrations.
entries.5937d76c0a52a3ff3e019b08c0bb366dc3564370: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen11135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11136" type="x-p"/> Because the Lord hath said - The particle וכי vechi should be translated for if, not because. For If the Lord hath said unto him, Curse David, who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so!
entries.689e387effd9aea9c3554b1c3a8b0cbdde6b159d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen11136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11137" type="x-p"/> Let him curse; for the Lord hath bidden him - No soul of man can suppose that ever God bade one man to curse another, much less that he commanded such a wretch as Shimei to curse such a man as David; but this is a peculiarity of the Hebrew language, which does not always distinguish between permission and commandment. Often the Scripture attributes to God what he only permits to be done; or what in the course of his providence he does not hinder. David, however, considers all this as being permitted of God for his chastisement and humiliation. I cannot withhold from my readers a very elegant poetic paraphrase of this passage, from the pen of the Rev. Charles Wesley, one of the first of Christian poets: - "Pure from the blood of Saul in vain, <div eID="gen11137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11138" type="x-p"/> He dares not to the charge reply: <div eID="gen11138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11139" type="x-p"/> Uriah's doth the charge maintain, <div eID="gen11139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11140" type="x-p"/> Uriah's doth against him cry! <div eID="gen11140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11141" type="x-p"/> Let Shimei curse: the rod he bears <div eID="gen11141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11142" type="x-p"/> For sins which mercy had forgiven: <div eID="gen11142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11143" type="x-p"/> And in the wrongs of man reveres <div eID="gen11143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11144" type="x-p"/> The awful righteousness of heaven. <div eID="gen11144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11145" type="x-p"/> Lord, I adore thy righteous will, <div eID="gen11145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11146" type="x-p"/> Through every instrument of ill <div eID="gen11146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11147" type="x-p"/> My Father's goodness see; <div eID="gen11147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11148" type="x-p"/> Accept the complicated wrong <div eID="gen11148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11149" type="x-p"/> Of Shimei's hand and Shimei's tongue <div eID="gen11149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11150" type="x-p"/> As kind rebukes from Thee.
entries.21d722774f18be4ed0410c9153f57244ad3d110f: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen11150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11151" type="x-p"/> The men of Israel - These words are wanting in the Chaldee, Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, and Arabic, and in two of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS.
entries.8f180ebaff6a60c78e38fe783cb0963df2990b2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen11151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11152" type="x-p"/> Whom the Lord and this people - choose - Here is an equivocation; Hushai meant in his heart that God and all the people of Israel had chosen David; but he spake so as to make Absalom believe that he spoke of him: for whatever of insincerity may appear in this, Hushai is alone answerable. What he says afterwards may be understood in the same way.
entries.65b2ba43b622ae21d377f77ac1655363c32cb3c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen11152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11153" type="x-p"/> Go in unto thy father's concubines - It may be remembered that David left ten of them behind to take care of the house, see <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.16">2Sam 15:16</reference>. Ahithophel advised this infernal measure, in order to prevent the possibility of a reconciliation between David and his son; thus was the prophecy to Nathan fulfilled, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.11">2Sam 12:11</reference>. And this was probably transacted in the very same place where David's eye took the adulterous view of Bath-sheba; see <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.2">2Sam 11:2</reference>. <div eID="gen11153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11154" type="x-p"/> The wives of the conquered king were always the property of the conqueror; and in possessing these, he appeared to possess the right to the kingdom. Herodotus informs us that Smerdis, having seized on the Persian throne after the death of Cambyses, espoused all the wives of his predecessor, lib. iii., c. 68. But for a son to take his father's wives was the sum of abomination, and was death by the law of God, <reference osisRef="Lev.20.11">Lev 20:11</reference>. This was a sin rarely found, even among the Gentiles. <div eID="gen11154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11155" type="x-p"/> Every part of the conduct of Absalom shows him to have been a most profligate young man; he was proud, vindictive, adulterous, incestuous, a parricide, and, in fine, reprobate to every good word and work. We still however recollect that David had grievously sinned, and we should also recollect that he suffered grievously for it; and that his humiliation, repentance, and amendment, were most decisive and exemplary. Reader, God is as just as he is merciful.  <chapter eID="2Sam.16"/> <div eID="gen11155" type="x-p"/>

entries.50cc05b2408ea41ed6ad4ec89a68213fef4fb146: <hi type="italic">Ziba’s faithless conduct towards Mephibosheth.</hi> - 2Sa 16:1. When David had gone a little over the height (of the Mount of Olives: הראשׁ points back to <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.32">2Sa 15:32</reference>), Mephibosheth’s servant Ziba came to meet him, with a couple of asses saddled, and laden with two hundred loaves, a hundred raisin-cakes, a hundred date or fig-cakes, and a skin of wine. The word קיץ corresponds to the Greek ὀπώρα, as the lxx have rendered it in <reference osisRef="Jer.40.10">Jer 40:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.40.12">Jer 40:12</reference>, and is used to signify summer fruits, both here and in <reference osisRef="Amos.8.1">Amo 8:1</reference> (Symm.). The early translators rendered it lumps of figs in the present passage (παλάθαι; cf. Ges<hi type="italic">. Thes</hi>. p. 1209). The Septuagint only has ἑκατὸν φοίνικες. The latter is certainly the more correct, as the dried lumps of figs or fig-cakes were called דּבלים   (<reference osisRef="1Sam.25.18">1Sa 25:18</reference>); and even at the present day ripe dates, pressed together in lumps like cakes, are used in journeys through the desert, as a satisfying and refreshing food (vid., Winer, <hi type="italic">bibl. Realwörterbuch</hi>, i. 253).
entries.e7e6ad1248d02c709b4f64a00950bda875f98817: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.2">2Sa 16:2</reference> <div eID="gen4471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4472" type="x-p"/> When the king asked him, <hi type="italic">“What are these for thee?”</hi> i.e., what art thou going to do with them? Ziba replied, “The asses are for the king’s family to ride upon (to ride upon in turn), the bread and summer fruits for the young men (the king’s servants) to eat, and the wine for those that are faint in the desert to drink” (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.23">2Sa 15:23</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> ולהלחם is evidently a copyist’s error for והלּחם.
entries.a39d2b47bc60ae675c761447724f82a0eaebb455: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.3">2Sa 16:3</reference> <div eID="gen4472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4473" type="x-p"/> To the further question put by the king, “Where is thy lord (Mephibosheth)? Ziba replied, “Behold, he sits (is staying) in Jerusalem; for he said, To-day will the house of Israel restore the kingship (government) of my father.” The <hi type="italic">“kingship of my father,”</hi> inasmuch as the throne would have passed to Jonathan if he had outlived Saul. It is obvious enough, apart altogether from 2Sa 19:25., the Ziba was calumniating his master Mephibosheth, in the hope of getting possession of the lands that he was farming for him. A cripple like Mephibosheth, lame in both feet, who had never put in any claim to the throne before, could not possibly have got the idea now that the people of Israel, who had just chosen Absalom as king, would give the throne of Saul to such a cripple as he was. It is true that Ziba’s calumny was very improbable; nevertheless, in the general confusion of affairs, it was not altogether an inconceivable thing that the oppressed party of Saul might avail themselves of this opportunity to make an attempt to restore the power of that house, which many greatly preferred to that of David, under the name of Mephibosheth.
entries.7ee842901aa1f31f707fc998bf8c816a641dfd7a: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.4">2Sa 16:4</reference> <div eID="gen4473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4474" type="x-p"/> And in the excited state in which David then was, he was weak enough to give credence to Ziba’s words, and to commit the injustice of promising the calumniator all that belonged to Mephibosheth, - a promise for which he most politely thanked him. השׁתּחויתי, <hi type="italic">“I bow myself,”</hi> equivalent to, I lay myself at thy feet. <hi type="italic">“May I find favour in the eyes of my lord the king!”</hi> i.e., may the king grant me his favour (vid., <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.18">1Sa 1:18</reference>).
entries.4d3453a096d32badfa8c6f8e5300d245e8c52e0b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5-2Sam.16.6">2Sa 16:5-6</reference> <hi type="italic">Shimei’s cursing.</hi> - <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.5">2Sa 16:5</reference>, 2Sa 16:6. When the king had come to <hi type="italic">Bahurim</hi>, on the other side of the Mount of Olives, but not far off (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.16">2Sa 3:16</reference>), there came out of that place a man of the family of the house of Saul, i.e., a distant relation of Saul, cursing him; and he pelted David and all his servants with stones, although all the people and all the heroes (the household troops and body-guard: <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.17-2Sam.15.18">2Sa 15:17-18</reference>) were (marking) on the right and left of the king. The words “all the people,” etc., are a circumstantial clause.
entries.831d55c498a82953dbac4948d797d08caca89a2d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.7-2Sam.16.8">2Sa 16:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen4474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4475" type="x-p"/> Shimei cursed thus: “<hi type="italic">Out, out</hi> (away, away), thou man of blood, and worthless man! Jehovah hath repaid thee (now) for all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose stead thou hast become king, and hath given the kingdom into the hand of Absalom thy son. Behold, now thou art in thy misfortune, for thou art a man of blood.” דּמים אישׁ, a man of drops of blood, i.e., one who has shed blood or committed murder. What Shimei meant by <hi type="italic">“all the blood of the house of Saul,”</hi> which David had shed, and because of which he was a man of blood, it is impossible to determine with certainty. He may possibly have attributed to David the murder of Ishbosheth and Abner, notwithstanding the fact that David was innocent of the death of both (see 2Sa 3:27., and 2Sa 4:6.). By <hi type="italic">“in whose stead thou hast reigned,”</hi> he meant whose throne thou hast forcibly usurped; and by בּרעתך הנּך, “it is for this that punishment hat overtaken thee now.”
entries.2dc0be4b598397652571660858e50bf388393832: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.9-2Sam.16.10">2Sa 16:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen4475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4476" type="x-p"/> Abishai wanted to put an end to this cursing (on the expression “dead dog,” see <reference osisRef="2Sam.9.8">2Sa 9:8</reference>). “Let me go,” said he to David, “and take away his head,” i.e., chop off his head. But David replied, “What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah?” Joab probably joined with Abishai. The formula “what to me and you?” signifies that a person did not wish to have anything in common with the feelings and views of another (cf. 1Ki 17:18; <reference osisRef="Josh.22.24">Jos 22:24</reference>; and τὶ ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί, Joh 2:4. For the thing itself, comp. <reference osisRef="Luke.9.52-Luke.9.56">Luk 9:52-56</reference>). “If he curses, and if Jehovah hath said to him, Curse David, who shall then say, Wherefore hast thou done so?” For יה וכי יקלּל כּי (<hi type="italic">Chethib</hi>), the Masoretes give us the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, יה כּי יקלּל כּה, “so let him curse, for Jehovah,” etc. This thought lies at the foundation of the rendering adopted by the lxx, who have inserted, by way of explanation, καὶ ἄφετε αὐτὸν καὶ: so let him go, and so may he curse. The Vulgate is just the same: <hi type="italic">dimittite eum ut maledicat</hi>. This interpolation is taken from <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.11">2Sa 16:11</reference>, and, like the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, is nothing more than a conjecture, which was adopted simply because כּי was taken as a causal particle, and then offence was taken at וכי. But כּי signifies if, <hi type="italic">quando</hi>, in this passage, and the ו before the following וּמי introduces the apodosis.
entries.54144c14e7edf351e5b3620f3e328ec0ee21cfdc: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.11-2Sam.16.12">2Sa 16:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen4476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4477" type="x-p"/> David said still further to Abishai and all his servants: “Behold, my own son seeketh after my life; how much more then the Benjaminite! (who belongs to a hostile race.) Let him curse, for Jehovah hath bidden him. Perhaps Jehovah will look upon my guilt, and Jehovah will requite me good for the curse which befals me this day.” בּעוני (<hi type="italic">Chethib</hi>) has been altered by the Masoretes into בּעיני o, “upon mine eye,” probably in the sense of “upon my tears;” and קללתי into קללתו, - from pure misapprehension. בּעוני does not mean “upon my misery,” for עון never has this meaning, but upon the guilt which really belongs to me, in contrast with that with which Shimei charges me; and קללתי is the curse that has come upon me. Although David had committed no murder upon the house of Saul, and therefore Shimei’s cursing was nothing but malicious blasphemy, he felt that it came upon him because of his sins, though not for the sin imputed to him. He therefore forbade their putting the blasphemer to death, and said Jehovah had commanded him to curse; regarding the cursing as the consequence of the wrath of God that was bringing him low (comp. the remarks on <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">1Sa 26:19</reference>). But this consciousness of guilt also excited the assurance that the Lord would look upon his sin. When God looks upon the guilt of a humble sinner, He will also, as a just and merciful God, avert the evil, and change the suffering into a blessing. David founded upon this the hope, that the Lord would repay him with good for the curse with which Shimei was pursuing him now.
entries.422bea7296903e9589b32d253c4945ecac1f9d1d: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.13">2Sa 16:13</reference> “So David went with his men on the way, whilst Shimei went on the slope of the hill opposite to him, cursing continually, and pelted with stones over against him, and with earth.” לעמּתו means over against him in both instances. It is not expressly stated that Shimei threw stones and earth at David, but this is implied in the context.
entries.47304cc060b58c4ef873ba9e9e149505597d9559: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.14">2Sa 16:14</reference> <div eID="gen4477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4478" type="x-p"/> The king came with his train, pursued in this manner, to Ayephim, and refreshed himself there. The context requires that <hi type="italic">Ayephim</hi> should be taken as the name of a place. If it were an appellative, signifying weary, there would be no information as to the place to which David came, and to which the word שׁם (there) distinctly refers. Bahurim cannot be the place alluded to, for the simple reason that, according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.18">2Sa 17:18</reference>, the place where David rested was a considerable distance beyond Bahurim, towards the Jordan, as we may see from the fact that it is stated there that the priests’ sons, who were sent to carry information to David of what was occurring in Jerusalem, hid themselves in a well at Bahurim from the officers who were following them, and consequently had to go still further in order to convey the news to David; so that it is out of the question to supply this name from 2Sa 16:5. It is true that we never meet with the name <hi type="italic">Ayephim</hi> again; but this applies to many other places whose existence is not called in question.<note placement="foot">The meaning of the word, wearied or weariness, does not warrant any conjectures, even though they should be more felicitous than that of Böttcher, who proposes to alter <hi type="italic">Ayephim</hi> into <hi type="italic">Ephraim</hi>, and assumes that there was a place of this name near Mahanaim, though without reflecting that the place where David rested was on this side of the Jordan, and somewhere near to Gilgal or Jericho (2Sa 17:16. and <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.22">2Sa 17:22</reference>).</note>
entries.7d04d54196e5ae99b67bbbb4a6a23cc8ad0e706b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.15-2Sam.16.16">2Sa 16:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen4478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4479" type="x-p"/> When Absalom and “all the people, the men of Israel,” i.e., the people who had joined him out of all the tribes of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.10">2Sa 15:10</reference>), came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him, Hushai the Archite also came and greeted him warmly as king, by exclaiming again and again, “Long live the king!”
entries.82f4b34dd0e932a698cc8a190fb8f7b6dca57f29: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.17-2Sam.16.19">2Sa 16:17-19</reference> <div eID="gen4479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4480" type="x-p"/> Absalom, apparently astonished at this, said to him, “Is this thy love to thy friend (David)? why wentest thou not with thy friend?” But Hushai replied, “No; but whom Jehovah hath chosen, and this people (i.e., the people who had entered Jerusalem with Absalom), and all the men of Israel (i.e., the whole nation), to him (לא for לו, <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>) will I belong, and will remain with him. And again, whom should I serve? Is it not before his son? As I have served thy father, so will I be before thee” (i.e., serve thee). With great craftiness, Hushai declared at the very outset that Jehovah had chosen Absalom - at least he could not come to any other conclusion, judging from the results. And under such circumstances he could not have any doubt as to whom it was his duty to serve. As he had formerly served the father, so now he would serve his son Absalom. In this way he succeeded in completely deceiving Absalom, so that he placed unbounded confidence in him.
entries.7a60eb9f5448f95ce868bec93264d8a94a17e13b: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.20">2Sa 16:20</reference> <div eID="gen4480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4481" type="x-p"/> After taking possession of the capital of the kingdom, the next thing to do was to form the resolution to take and keep the throne. Absalom therefore turned to Ahithophel, and said, “Give ye counsel what we are to do.” The plural הבוּ (give ye) may be explained on the supposition that the other persons present were addressed as well as Ahithophel, as being capable of giving advice.
entries.241eb350489e9e674e8f8fb8ce1656e3e8959d05: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.21">2Sa 16:21</reference> <div eID="gen4481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4482" type="x-p"/> Ahithophel gave the following counsel: “Go to thy father’s concubines, whom he hath left behind to keep the house (i.e., lie with them: for אל בּוא, compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.7">2Sa 3:7</reference>, etc.); so will all Israel hear that thou hast made thyself stinking with thy father, and the hands of all those who are with thee will strengthen themselves.” This advice was sagacious enough. Lying with the king’s concubines was an appropriation of the royal harem, and, as such, a complete usurpation of the throne (see at <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.7">2Sa 3:7</reference>), which would render any reconciliation between Absalom and his father utterly impossible, and therefore would of necessity instigate the followers of Absalom to maintain his cause with all the greater firmness. This was what Ahithophel hoped to attain through his advice. For unless the breach was too great to be healed, with the affection of David towards his sons, which might in reality be called weakness, it was always a possible thing that he should forgive Absalom; and in that case Ahithophel would be the one to suffer. But under the superintendence of God this advice of Ahithophel was to effect the fulfilment, without any such intention on his part, of the threat held over David in 2Sa 12:8.
entries.bc90913914bfe99fdc8de406273ea9c819e04270: <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.22-2Sam.16.23">2Sa 16:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen4482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4483" type="x-p"/> Absalom had a tent put up on the roof of the king’s palace, that his going in to the concubines might be done publicly in the sight of all Israel. For (as the historian adds in <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.23">2Sa 16:23</reference> by way of explanation) the counsel of Ahithophel, which he counselled in those days, was like a divine oracle both with David and with Absalom. The words from ועצת to ההם are placed at the commencement absolutely: “and (as for) the counsel of Ahithophel, ... as if one inquired the word of God, so was every counsel of Ahithophel.” The Masoretes have supplied אישׁ as the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> to ישׁאל. This is correct so far as the sense is concerned, but it is quite unnecessary, as ישׁאל may be taken impersonally. האלהים בּדבר שׁאל is to be explained from the formula בּעלהים שׁאל (see at Jdg 1:1).  <chapter eID="2Sam.16"/> <div eID="gen4483" type="x-p"/>

                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:261" />18 And Hushai said unto Absalom, Nay, but whom the LORD, and this people, and all the men of Israel chuse <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Though as a private person, I owed and payed Friend<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ship to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> whilest he was King; yet I must make all my Obligations give place to the Authority of God, who putteth down, and setteth up Kings at his pleasure; and to the common Sence and Decree of the whole Body of the Nation. But <ns0:hi>Hushai</ns0:hi> expresseth himself very cautiously; for though he would be thought to understand <ns0:hi>Absalom,</ns0:hi> yet in truth this Character did not agree to him, whom neither God, nor all the People had chosen, but onely a part, and that the worst part of them.</ns0:note>, his will I be, and with him will I abide.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19.                   <ns0:p n="20">20 Then said Absalom to Ahitophel, Give counsel among you what we shall do.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And Ahitophel said unto Absalom, Go in unto thy fathers concubines <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This Counsel he gave, partly to Revenge the Injury done to <ns0:hi>Bathsheba,</ns0:hi> who was the Daughter of <ns0:hi>Eliam,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 11. 3. who was <ns0:hi>the Son of Ahitophel, Chap.</ns0:hi> 23. 34. and prin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cipally, for his own, and the Peoples safety, that the Breach between <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> might be made wide, and irre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parable by so Vile an Action; which must needs provoke <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> in the highest Degree, both for the Sin, and shame of it; as the like Action had done <ns0:hi>Iacob, Gen.</ns0:hi> 49. 3, 4. and cut off all hopes of Reconciliation, which otherwise might have been expected by some Treaty between <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> and his render-hearted Father; in which Case his Followers, and especially <ns0:hi>Ahitophel</ns0:hi> himself, had been left to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Mercy.</ns0:note>, which he hath left to keep the house, and all Israel shall hear that thou <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> stinkest with thy fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther.</ns0:note> art abhorred of thy father <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">And therefore obliged by thy own Interest to Prosecute the War with all possible Vigor, and to abandon all thoughts of Peace: as knowing that his Father, though he might dissemble, yet would never forgive so foul and scandalous a Crime. Yea, they will Fight with greater Courage and Resolu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, when they are freed from the fear of thy Reconciliati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, which otherwise would make their Hearts saint, and Hands slack in thy Cause. But by this we may see the Cha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />racter of <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s Party, and how abominably wicked they were, whom such a loathsome and Scandalous Action tied the faster to him, whom for that very reason they should have deserted and abhorred. And we may further learn, how corrupt and filthy the Body of the People was, and how ripe for that severe judgment which is now hastening to them.</ns0:note>, then shall the hands of all that <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> with thee be strong <ns0:hi>e.</ns0:hi>
